paragraphs: Chemistry is the study of what things are made of and how they change. Everything you can touch, from the water in a glass to the metal in a spoon, is built from a small set of ingredients called elements, joined together in different ways. People study chemistry to explain why salt dissolves, why a flame needs air, and how much of one substance it takes to react with another. Cooking, medicine, batteries and cleaning products all rest on it.

The course has 12 lessons in four parts. Meet the particles looks inside a single atom and at what makes one element differ from another. Build a connection shows how atoms join, by handing electrons over or by sharing them. Count a substance introduces the mole, a unit for counting enormous numbers of atoms at once, so that you can weigh out an exact amount of a chemical. Follow a reaction uses those tools to balance equations and to work out what runs out first.
Chemistry here is quantitative, so most lessons have you work something out with numbers, and many have figures of atoms and molecules to explore. Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell which element an atom is, and work out its neutrons, electrons and charge from a few counts.
You'll be able to write the formula of an ionic compound from the charges on its ions.
You'll be able to find the mass of a given amount of a substance, and the amount from a mass, using atomic masses and the mole.
You'll be able to balance a chemical equation so that every atom is accounted for.
You'll be able to say which reactant runs out first and how much product a reaction can make.
prerequisites: You should be comfortable with multiplying, dividing and simple fractions, which is all the maths the course assumes.
